Twenty-five comments

The Nine Points of Roguery

A great set of notes to go with a wonderful title. The B part, with it’s c natural, is the signature of this three part reel.

If you don’t want the triplets in the A part, just play them as FD. Similarly, you can skip the rolls on the c and B in the B Part by simply playing |=c2 cA B2 BG|. The rest of the tune is pretty straightforward.

↳ Posted by Kenny on October 13th, 2008.

@Greg t P T

C nat roll is played fingering the C nat with the two index fingers up (everything else down), closing the right index finger to play the upper note of the ornament and closing the left index finger to play the lower. Sounds good if done quickly.

What are the Nine Points of Roguery?

1. deceit
2. slight of hand
3. cunning
4. influence
5. a comely face
6. upper hand
7. good natured (hint of cynicism optional)
8. loadsa style
9. perfectly ruthless (can play the bagpipe and will)

Well, I’m only guessing… Any specialist out there?

Re: The Nine Points Of Roguery

I suspect that the original form of the title was “Nine Points of Roguery” and was intended as a comic opposition to William Murray, Lord Mansfield’s famous phrase “property is nine points of the law” (usually misquoted these days in modern legal language as “possession is nine-tenths of the law”).

↳ Posted by myles on December 27th, 2016.

John Doherty’s story

Transcription of John Doherty’s story from the video linked above:
______________________________
Yes, yes, I can tell you a story about what happened one time in Fanad. It was about a horse rider that was coming home from Letterkenny, on his way going to Fanad, and - that was a true story, that wasn’t a ‘yarn’, as we say, that was a real true story - and this rider was coming right down, on and on, till he came to a crossroads somewhere between Milford and Fanad. And that crossroads, that was talked about over the county, all about this strange vision that was always seen [at the] crossroads.

And as Doyle was coming down on horseback, somewhere at a little distance he saw the vision standing at the crossroads. And it was Sally he called the mare - she was a black mare without a white hair - and as he saw the vision standing at the crossroads the poor soul had nothing to do, and he just pull the reins and tell Sally to go on. So, the mare did go on with a rapid dash, and passed the vision, and the vision kept on the road with the mare, all until they went into Fanad. And it was a long, long, long, tough race - the vision kept with the mare but she still led the vision out.

And on and on and on and on till they came near to Doyle’s house. Doyle was a good fiddle player. And when he came in he was badly excited, and he rested for a while - he put the mare into the stable and he rested for a while after that - and he came into the kitchen and he took his supper. [I can’t make out this sentence - ‘in a kind of way, badly ____ though’ ?] And some time after that he prepared to go to bed.

Well, he went into bed, and somehow he couldn’t sleep. He was thinking of just his experience, about this terrible vision that he had seen. And the rhythm of the mare’s hooves on the road give Doyle the impression of this reel that he was about to play on the fiddle. So he lay on the bed for a while, and he woke up then after a sort of a slumber, and he reached for the fiddle and he took down the fiddle, and played this reel over and over - three or four times over - again, and he had no name for the reel but the name he called it was the Black Mare of Fanad. That’s the name he give the reel.

Now, sometimes people - very smart lads maybe - some of them maybe call this, give it a different name, maybe they would call it ‘The Nine Points of Roguery’, some name like that you know? But the real name of the reel is the Black Mare of Fanad.
______________________________

I can’t tell if it’s just Doherty’s accent or if he actually says ‘give’ where you would usually say ‘gave’!

Doherty’s rendition of the tune has always seemed to me to have a real edge to it, for want of a better word, and no wonder when you consider this story that he associated with it. His version is closest to X:3 posted by jardineromi; that phrase in bars 3-4 with the leap of a seventh and the subsequent C natural feels like a wonderfully wild touch, bearing that haunting quality.
